newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia keeps row with Singapore simmering.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia keeps row with Singapore simmering.

text.p: Youth politicians in Malaysia demanded an apology from Singapore's deputy prime minister on Thursday as a row bubbled on over remarks about a Malaysian state made by his father.

Deputy Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong should also apologise to Malaysia for the disparaging remarks made by his father, Senior Minister Lee Kuan Yew, the youth wing of Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad's party said.

"As a neighbouring country, it is hard for us to accept the reality that our closest neighbour has stabbed from the back," said Ahmad Zahid Hamidi, the youth chief of Mahathir's United Malays National Organisation (UMNO).
Lee described the Malaysian state of Johor as "notorious for shootings, muggings and car-jackings" in a court affidavit filed against Singapore opposition politican Tang Liang Hong.
Zahid said Lee Hsien Loong should also apologise as he had joined his father in filing the affidavit.
Tang fled to Johor in January, saying he feared for his life after losing a parliamentary race in Singapore's elections.
Lee said on Monday he had instructed his lawyers to ask the court to delete the offending remarks from the record.
Foreign Minister Abdullah Badawi said on Wednesday Malaysia welcomed Lee's move to withdraw the statement, but that "restoration of the old level of relationship would take time".
Singapore Foreign Minister Shanmugam Jayakumar said he was "surprised" by Abdullah's statement on the future of ties.
Zahid took a swipe at Jayakumar for that statement as well.

"The Foreign Minister should not try to teach Malaysia how to establish diplomatic ties. His shocking statement showed how the republic's leaders failed to value the historical ties between the two countries," Zahid said.
About a dozen activists, meanwhile, protested outside the Singapore high commission in Kuala Lumpur on Thursday against what they viewed as "persecution of political opposition" in Singapore.

Wearing black handkerchiefs over their faces, the protesters said the row "has distracted attention from the real issue -- the systematic persecution of those who dare to express opinions contrary to the PAP (Peoples Action Party) government".
The protesters said they wore handkerchiefs to prevent them from being identified by high commission staff, who were seen photographing and videotaping the demonstration.
They said in a statement the 13 libel suits that have been filed against Tang were not an isolated incident.

"Other political opponents of the PAP had been hounded out of the country. These include student leader Tan Wah Piow, former Solicitor General Francis Seow, former President Devan Nair and many others," the statement said.
Police stood by as the protest went on for half an hour.
Demonstrations in Malaysia are technically illegal under emergency laws.

Any sort of protest against a fellow member of the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) -- Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam -- is almost never tolerated.
